shorts.angle: The debt began at about two thousand three hundred dollars and grew itself into roughly fifteen thousand through penalty, interest and fees — and two federal courts dismissed her before anyone would look.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What the highest court in the country said about a debt that had multiplied itself six times over.

lines.text: The bill that cost Geraldine Tyler her home was about two thousand three hundred dollars. The price of a used car.
source_lines: Her tax had gone unpaid — not a fortune, not a mansion's worth of back taxes. About two thousand three hundred dollars.
About two thousand three hundred dollars. [CLM-0004] The price of a used car.

lines.text: An unpaid tax bill does not sit and wait. It grows. The county added a penalty, then interest, then costs, and fees on top.
source_lines: And this is where the machine begins to hum — because an unpaid tax bill does not simply sit and wait. It grows. The county added a penalty. Then interest. Then costs, and fees layered on top of the costs, month after month, quarter after quarter, with no hand anywhere on the brake.

lines.text: By the time anyone read the figure back to her, twenty-three hundred dollars had swollen to roughly fifteen thousand. More than six times over.
source_lines: By the time anyone read the figure back to her, twenty-three hundred dollars had swollen to roughly fifteen thousand.

lines.text: Not because she borrowed a dollar more, or gambled, or spent, or ran. The clock kept running, and the law let it run.
source_lines: The debt had multiplied more than six times over — not because she borrowed a single dollar more, not because she gambled or spent or ran, but because the clock kept running and the law let it run.

lines.text: She had already paid the condo off. The deed was clean. Owning it outright was supposed to be the safe part.
source_lines: She had bought that little place in Minneapolis and made it hers one payment at a time, over years of ordinary work, until the loan was gone and the deed was clean.
She had done the hard thing. She had finished. And the finishing did not save her.

lines.text: At first, the law did not agree with her. The federal district court dismissed her case in 2020. She appealed.

lines.text: In 2022 the federal court of appeals affirmed that dismissal. The same answer, one level higher up. Two courts. Two losses.

lines.text: She was not asking for the home back. Only the change: the difference between the small debt and the value the county had pocketed.
